summary: Comers Rock lookout on Iron Mountain, Jefferson National Forest: 1931 wooden cab, sold 1956; site is now a public overlook with a concrete slab and stone pillars.

facts.design: 19 by 14 foot wooden cab on a stone foundation
facts.status_note: Cab sold to a private party in 1956; the register describes a concrete slab with stone pillars and wooden rails at the site

access.note: Register calls it a public scenic lookout within the Mount Rogers National Recreation Area; the Forest Service runs a campground and overlook there

visit.trail_note: Long-distance hikes in the Little Dry Run Wilderness are within walking distance of the campground (Forest Service)

events.note: Register says the wooden cab on a stone foundation was built in 1931
1934 Appalachian Trail guide, as a local history recounts it, describes a fire tower at the summit
Cab sold to a private party (Register); a Forest Lookouts entry says a private party purchased the site
1960s: site remodeled into the observation platform (local history, citing Forest Service documents); year is approximate

evidence.supports: built 1931 as a wooden cab on a stone foundation
evidence.quote: This 19'x14' wooden cab on stone foundation was built 1931 on Comers Rock

evidence.supports: cab sold to a private party in 1956; site now a public scenic lookout
evidence.quote: The cab was sold to a private party in 1956, but the site is now a public scenic lookout.

evidence.supports: concrete slab on the footer; stone pillars with wooden rails
evidence.quote: A concrete slab was poured on top of the footer, and on top of that were built stone pillars with wooden rails between them.

evidence.supports: part of the Mount Rogers National Recreation Area within the Jefferson National Forest
evidence.quote: The lookout is now part of the Mount Rogers National Recreation Area, which lies within the Jefferson National Forest.

evidence.supports: Register places the summit in Wythe County
evidence.quote: the highest point in Wythe County

evidence.supports: administered by the U.S. Forest Service
a private party purchased the site of the lookout in 1956
evidence.quote: 1956: A private party purchased the site of the lookout.

evidence.supports: 1934 trail guide describes a fire tower at the summit
evidence.quote: By 1934, an Appalachian Trail guide described a Forest Service trail following the crest of Iron Mountain for nearly four miles to the summit of Comers Rock, where hikers encountered a fire tower.

evidence.supports: Forest Service documents describe the overlook as a 1930s development used as a fire tower
evidence.quote: Forest Service documents likewise describe the Comers Rock overlook as a 1930s development that was used as a fire tower.
In the 1960s, the site was remodeled into the observation platform familiar to later visitors.

evidence.supports: local history places the community in northern Grayson County
evidence.quote: The community lies in northern Grayson County

evidence.supports: Forest Service recreation page: campground, overlook, former fire tower views, Little Dry Run Wilderness hikes
evidence.quote: Within walking distance of the campground are long distance hikes in Little Dry Run Wilderness, 360 degree views from Comers Rock Overlook and former fire tower

evidence.supports: primitive campground and historic picnic area on Iron Mountain
evidence.quote: a small primitive campground and historic picnic area await the true outdoor enthusiast

sources.title: Comers Rock, Grayson County: From an 1860 Post Office to the Appalachian Trail

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Register and Forest Lookouts list Wythe County; the local history places the community in northern Grayson County. The brief keeps Wythe; the story gives both.
Register says the cab was sold to a private party; Forest Lookouts says a private party purchased the site. The story gives the Register's wording and notes the other.

notes_for_editor: Four sources. No staffing or fire-event sources found in two searches, so none are included. Built year 1931 is from the Register; the local history says 1930s. The brief record had no built event; added. The Register says only that the cab was sold, so the story does not say where the cab went. Site description today comes from the Register and the Forest Service page; the local history's 1960s observation platform is consistent with both.
